clue.text: Doctors' bills cause such outcry!

definitions.meaning: charlatan medics, or slang for doctors in general; the possessive is the surface's, the sense is plural doctors
the bills here are ducks' beaks, and the noisy outcry they make is the duck's call

explanation.surface: A complaint that medical fees provoke loud public protest.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'bills' as invoices from doctors; the second reading makes them a duck's beak, whose outcry is its call.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for doctors, especially unqualified ones, and also the plural of the noise a duck makes.

clue.text: One addicted to American TV series

parts.note: ER was a long-running American hospital drama on television

explanation.surface: Someone hooked on a US television drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A drug user is someone with a habit, so a person addicted to something.

clue.text: Officer doubly correct to provide protection

parts.note: a cop is a police officer
correct twice over: Y as the mark for yes on a form, then right meaning correct
correct twice over: Y as the mark for yes on a form, then right meaning correct

explanation.surface: A police officer being twice as proper in order to guard someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doubly correct' gives two words for correct: Y (as in yes) and RIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal ownership of a creative work shields it from being reproduced without permission, a form of protection.

clue.text: Monster's swaying hips gets knight cross

indicators.note: hips that sway move about, so the letters of hips are rearranged

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight
a cross is drawn as the letter X

explanation.surface: A beast whose swinging hips make a knight angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swaying' shuffles HIPS into SPHI. 'cross' looks like an adjective (angry) but is the X shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A mythical beast with a lion's body and a human head, a monster of Greek legend.

clue.text: "An Englishman in New York" from Elton? Nonsense!

parts.note: Elton John, the singer, supplies his surname
bull is slang, chiefly American, for rubbish or nonsense

explanation.surface: A query whether Elton John sang Sting's song about an Englishman in New York, dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in New York' hints that the nonsense word is American slang. The quoted title is Sting's song 'Englishman in New York', not one of Elton John's.
explanation.definitionFit: The cartoon figure personifying England, and so a typical Englishman.

clue.text: India's Koh-i-noor?

parts.note: India was called the most prized possession of the British Empire, and the Koh-i-noor diamond, taken from India, is set in the British crown

explanation.surface: A question about the famous Indian diamond.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works twice: India was the Empire's most prized colony, and the Koh-i-noor is literally a gem in the Queen Mother's crown.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for the most valuable part of a collection, applied to both India and the diamond.

clue.text: US strikes hard: Republican peacekeepers are in some trouble

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: the Republican and the peacekeepers are placed inside the other letters
the word some, in trouble, is stirred up and rearranged

parts.note: the UN, United Nations, sends peacekeeping forces

explanation.surface: American military strikes, with Republicans and UN troops caught in difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strikes' suggests military attacks, but these are baseball hits. 'trouble' rearranges some, and 'are in' places the Republican and peacekeepers inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: In baseball, hits that let the batter round all the bases are the big strikes of the American game.

clue.text: Back massage with spirit to cover the whole body

indicators.note: read back, the word for massage runs from right to left

parts.note: to rub is to massage
the ka is the soul or spirit in ancient Egyptian belief

explanation.surface: A back rub with a drink, then wrapping up from head to toe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like the body part being massaged; it turns RUB into BUR.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose garment worn by some Muslim women, made to cover them from head to foot.

clue.text: Slave's uprising about iron regularly fears tropical disease

indicators.note: the reversed servant goes round the symbol for iron
in a down entry, rising reads the word from the bottom up, so backwards

parts.note: a vassal is a feudal servant, a slave to his lord
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

indicators.note: taking every other letter of fears, the second and fourth

explanation.surface: A slave revolt and fears of a tropical illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'uprising' turns VASSAL into LASSAV, which goes 'about' FE: LASSA(FE)V, then ER from 'regularly fears'.
explanation.definitionFit: A viral haemorrhagic fever found in West Africa, named after a town in Nigeria: a tropical illness.

clue.text: Captive hugging frisky sheep? It's erotic to some …

indicators.note: the captive's letters wrap round the others

parts.note: a POW is a prisoner of war

indicators.note: frisky sheep jump about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A prisoner cuddling a lively sheep, which some find a turn-on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frisky' shuffles SHEEP into EEPSH, which POW hugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A titillating show watched through a small hole, which is erotic entertainment for some viewers.

clue.text: … perhaps, holding nothing is gloomy

indicators.note: the code's name holds the zero inside it

parts.note: three dots are the letter S in Morse code, so the dots are an example of Morse
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: an empty peep show is depressing.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis seems only to link to the previous clue, but three dots spell S in Morse code, so it stands for MORSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sullen and melancholy in mood, a synonym for downcast.

clue.text: Incredibly, an old age actor finally ran for president

indicators.note: an unbelievable arrangement, so the letters are rearranged
finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the word actor is used

explanation.surface: An elderly actor surprisingly stood for the presidency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incredibly' shuffles AN OLD AGE, R (actor's last letter) and RAN together.
explanation.definitionFit: The film actor who became the fortieth American head of state in 1981.

clue.text: Short of time, they run about in stadia

definitions.text: Short of time, they run about in stadia

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are put inside the sports venues

parts.note: stadiums are sports grounds

indicators.note: letters that run about are rearranged
lacking, so the time letter is removed from they

explanation.surface: Athletes rushing round stadiums against the clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short of time' takes T from THEY, leaving HEY; 'run about' shuffles it to EYH, which goes 'in' GROUNDS. The whole clue also describes racing dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast racing dogs that chase a lure round oval tracks in dog-racing stadiums.

clue.text: Jumper for playing golf

indicators.note: the letters of for are played about with, so rearranged

parts.note: Golf is the radio alphabet code word for G

explanation.surface: A sweater to wear on the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' suggests a sweater (British for pullover) but is a creature that jumps. 'playing' shuffles FOR into FRO.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphibian known for leaping, so literally something that jumps.

clue.text: Back in goal with utter ease, bearing number

indicators.note: the word in is turned back to front

parts.note: the net is the goal in football

indicators.note: uttered aloud, the word ease sounds like the letters E's

parts.note: said out loud, ease is the same as E's, two Es
N, north, is a compass bearing

explanation.surface: Scoring easily while carrying a shirt number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in' gives NI; 'utter ease' says ease aloud, which sounds like E's, giving EE.
explanation.definitionFit: Nineteen is a whole number, between eighteen and twenty.

clue.text: In the US, rank and duty — it's an order by duke

parts.note: a duty is a tax on goods

indicators.note: putting letters in order rearranges them

explanation.surface: An order from a duke about rank and obligation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'order' rearranges IT'S AN into ISTAN. A taxi rank, in British English, is where taxis queue.
explanation.definitionFit: The American name for a place where cabs queue for passengers, what Britons call a cab rank.

clue.text: Doormen supply deliveries

definitions.meaning: door staff at clubs who throw out troublemakers
in cricket, short-pitched balls that rear up at the batter are a kind of delivery

explanation.surface: Door staff who provide delivery services.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a delivery is a ball bowled; a fast short one that rears up is a bouncer.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nightclub security staff and short, rising balls bowled in cricket.

clue.text: Canine, beginning to eat, still has nothing to go with hot stew

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter of eat is taken

parts.note: yet means still, as in not yet
O looks like zero, nothing

indicators.note: a stew mixes its ingredients, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A dog starting to eat a hot stew that has nothing more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stew' looks like the dog's food but shuffles YET, O, TO and H into YETOOTH.
explanation.definitionFit: The canine tooth in the upper jaw, the pointed one beneath the eye; canine is its formal name.

clue.text: Superheroes, followers of Ximenes' lead?

indicators.note: the leading letter of Ximenes

parts.note: men are followers, as an officer's men

explanation.surface: Superheroes who follow the rules of Ximenes, the crossword setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Ximenes was a famous Observer crossword setter whose rules for fair clues are followed by many setters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marvel comic team of mutant crime fighters, a group of comic-book heroes.

clue.text: Very much against the pointless subject of "rickrolling"

parts.note: V is short for versus, against

indicators.note: without a compass point, so the east letter is dropped

parts.note: rickrolling is the internet prank of linking to Rick Astley's song Never Gonna Give You Up

explanation.surface: Strongly opposed to the online prank's tedious target.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pointless' removes a compass point, E, from ASTLEY.
explanation.definitionFit: Immensely or hugely, an adverb of great degree.

clue.text: Those in society on form

parts.note: a machine that is on is working
a form is a class in a school

explanation.surface: Members of high society measured by their form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on form' looks like a phrase about performing well; ON is WORKING, and FORM is a school class (British usage).
explanation.definitionFit: The manual labourers are a stratum of society, the people in that social group.

clue.text: Bear a left, then a right, then reverse

indicators.note: the whole string built so far is turned round at the end

parts.note: OK means right, all correct

explanation.surface: Boxing instructions: a left, a right, then back off.
explanation.walkthrough: A, L, A, OK read backwards; 'then reverse' acts on all four pieces, not just the last.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian marsupial is popularly called a bear, though it is not one.

clue.text: In Belize, a lover showing passion

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words Belize, a lover

explanation.surface: A lover in Belize showing ardour.
explanation.definitionFit: Fervour or great enthusiasm, a synonym for ardour.

clue.text: Bad idea to restrain navy against attack

indicators.note: the shuffled idea holds the navy and against letters
a bad idea is a broken one, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: V is short for versus, against

explanation.surface: A foolish plan to hold back a fleet that opposes an attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' shuffles IDEA into IADE, which holds N and V: I(NV)ADE.
explanation.definitionFit: To march into enemy territory, to make an assault on it.

clue.text: Scott's companion, devouring lots of dessert and biscuits

indicators.note: the companion's name swallows the dessert's letters

parts.note: Captain Oates was on Scott's ill-fated Antarctic expedition

indicators.note: most of, so the last letter is cut

parts.note: cake is a dessert

explanation.surface: An explorer's companion eating plenty of pudding and biscuits.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Oates was the member of Scott's 1912 South Pole party who walked out into the blizzard. 'lots of' means nearly all, so the dessert loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat Scottish oat crackers, eaten like savoury biscuits.

clue.text: When special army group is retired with new killer?

parts.note: as means when, as in as I left
the SAS, Special Air Service, is a British army special forces unit

indicators.note: something retired has gone back, so the word is reads backwards

explanation.surface: A question about when a special forces unit stands down with a new killer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns IS into SI.
explanation.definitionFit: A hired or political murderer, so a killer.

clue.text: Sings flowing melody on Sunday without mass

indicators.note: letters that flow move freely, so they are rearranged
the mass letter is taken out of melody

parts.note: M is the symbol for mass in physics

explanation.surface: A choir singing a flowing tune on Sunday without a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mass' looks like the church service but is M, removed from MELODY; 'flowing' shuffles ELODY into YODEL.
explanation.definitionFit: Singing in the Alpine style, swinging between chest voice and falsetto.
